intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “C. S. Lewis (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of Jack Lewis, a book-loving boy from Belfast who stopped believing in God, was found by him again, and grew up to write the Chronicles of Narnia. It works for a small family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and suits children aged 6 to 12.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s short prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand so nothing in it takes you by surprise, and have paper, pencils and crayons ready. Jack’s story includes his mother’s death, the First World War and, at the end, the death of his wife Joy, so read those parts calmly, answer questions simply and truthfully without adding detail, never ask a child to share their own losses in front of the group, and keep coming back to the book’s own point: God never stopped looking for Jack, and he held on to him on happy days and sad ones.

weeks.summary: Clive Staples Lewis is born in Belfast in 1898 and soon insists on being called Jacksie, after a neighbour’s dog, which becomes Jack. He and his brother Warnie are best friends; a tiny moss garden on a biscuit-tin lid gives Jack a strange, sweet longing that returns all his life, and together the boys invent a pretend world called Boxen. At Little Lea, a house full of books, he reads and reads, and his parents take him to church and teach him to pray. The big idea: what we learn about God when we are small is like a seed, and God knows how to make it grow, even many years later.

memory_verse.text: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

activity.title: A Biscuit-Tin Garden
steps: Draw a big circle to be the lid of a biscuit tin.
Fill it with a tiny garden of moss, twigs and flowers, like the one Warnie made.
Draw three little seeds in the soil, and beside each write or draw one thing you have learned about God.
Write “God makes seeds grow” around the edge, and take your garden home.

weeks.summary: When Jack is nine, his mother becomes very ill with cancer; he prays with all his heart for her to get well, but she dies in August 1908. His father is too full of sadness to comfort the boys, so Jack and Warnie hold on to each other, and within a month they are sent to a harsh boarding school in England, where Jack nonetheless begins for a while to pray seriously. Years later, remembering how it felt, Jack wrote kind letters to many sad people. This chapter may touch children who have lost someone, or whose family member is ill: read it gently, do not explain why the prayer was not answered beyond what the chapter says (God did not stop the sad thing, but he was with Jack), and never ask anyone to talk about their own losses aloud. The big idea: when we are sad, God is close to us.

memory_verse.text: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

activity.title: Ways to Help a Sad Friend
steps: Remind the children how Jack and Warnie held on to each other when they were sad.
Sit in a circle and go round, each saying one kind thing you could do for a friend who is sad, such as sitting with them or drawing them a picture. Anyone may pass.
Say the memory verse together slowly.
Be quiet for half a minute, and silently ask God to comfort anyone you know who is sad.

weeks.summary: Somewhere between twelve and fourteen, worn out by worrying that his prayers did not count unless he felt exactly the right feelings, Jack quietly stops believing in God. He finds a lifelong friend in Arthur Greeves, learns to think clearly and to read many languages with his sharp teacher Mr Kirkpatrick, the Great Knock, and buys Phantastes by George MacDonald at a station, a story that touches his heart with a new kind of goodness. Leaders may want to reassure children that prayer does not depend on getting our feelings exactly right. The big idea: God can use teachers, friends and good books to help us, even before we know he is at work.

memory_verse.text: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.

activity.title: What Do You Mean By…?
steps: Tell the children how the Great Knock stopped Jack and asked what he meant by “wild.”
Say a simple sentence, such as “This room is big” or “That was a good day.”
Let the children ask, “What do you mean by big?” and help them give a careful, clear answer.
Take turns letting children say a sentence for the others to question, then thank God for people who help us think.

weeks.summary: Jack goes to Oxford in 1917 and, though he does not have to, joins the army; he shares a room with Paddy Moore, and the two promise that whoever survives the war will look after the other’s parent. Jack reaches the trenches in France on his nineteenth birthday, is wounded by a shell in April 1918, and the kind sergeant beside him is killed; Paddy is killed too. Keep the war part brief and calm, without adding detail, and steer the talk towards the promise rather than the fighting; children with family in the forces may need a quiet word afterwards. The big idea: even before Jack believed, God was holding his life in his hands, and a promise matters.

memory_verse.text: When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.

activity.title: A Promise I Can Keep
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
On the front, draw two hands shaking, the way friends do when they make a promise.
Inside, write or draw one small promise you can really keep this week, such as tidying your room or helping someone at home.
Sign your name under it, and take it home to remind you.

weeks.summary: Mrs Moore visits Jack in hospital when his own father does not come, and after the war Jack keeps his promise to Paddy, making his home with Mrs Moore and Maureen and looking after Mrs Moore for more than thirty years: shopping, washing dishes, walking the dog and studying when he can. He also does something wrong, hiding the truth from his father for years, and later he was very sorry for it. He works hard and becomes a teacher at Magdalen College in 1925. If you talk about saying sorry, keep it general and let any personal sorry stay between each child and God. The big idea: God wants us to be faithful and honest, and when we get it wrong, we can tell him we are sorry.

memory_verse.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

activity.title: Helping Hands Mime
steps: Remind the children of the jobs Jack did at home: shopping, washing dishes, running errands, walking the dog and helping Maureen with her Latin.
Let one child at a time mime one of those jobs, or another helpful job, while the others guess what it is.
Give everyone a turn, or let children mime in pairs if the group is large.
Finish by each choosing, silently, one job to do at home this week without being asked.

weeks.summary: At Oxford Jack makes friends, among them J. R. R. Tolkien, and is bothered that so many of the people and books he loves best are Christian; it feels as if God is hunting him. In 1929 his father dies before Jack can reach him, and Jack is sorry for how he often treated him. Then, alone in his room, he kneels and admits that God is God, calling himself “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England,” though he does not yet believe in Jesus. Mention the father’s death simply, as the chapter does. The big idea: nobody can run so far that God cannot find them.

memory_verse.text: Where could I go from your Spirit? Or where could I flee from your presence?

activity.title: Warmer, Colder
activity.materials: One small object, such as a crayon
steps: Send one child out of the room or ask them to close their eyes while you hide a crayon somewhere safe.
Bring them back and let the group guide them with “warmer” when they get closer and “colder” when they move away.
Play a few rounds so different children get a turn to search.
Talk about how the crayon could not stay hidden for ever, and how God kept looking for Jack until he found him.

weeks.summary: Jack believes in God but cannot understand Jesus. On a long night walk by the river in 1931, Tolkien and Hugo Dyson help him see that the story of Jesus is like the old stories he loves of a god who dies and comes back to life, with one great difference: it really happened. Nine days later, riding in the sidecar of Warnie’s motorcycle to Whipsnade Zoo, Jack comes to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and that Christmas he takes Communion, now sharing his faith with Warnie too. The big idea: the story of Jesus is not just beautiful; it is true, because God really came into our world.

memory_verse.text: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

activity.title: From the River to the Zoo
steps: Draw a winding path along a river, with three friends walking and talking under the night sky.
Carry the path on to a road, and draw a motorcycle with a sidecar and Jack riding in it.
At the end of the road, draw the zoo gate, and write next to it “It really happened!”
Share your maps in pairs and tell each other one true thing about Jesus.

weeks.summary: Jack, Warnie and Mrs Moore buy the Kilns, a brick house with woods and a pond, where Jack lives for the rest of his life; Warnie leaves the army and joins them, and every Sunday Jack walks to the early service at Holy Trinity, where he is simply Mr Lewis from the Kilns. On Thursday evenings his friends the Inklings meet in his rooms to read their writing aloud and say honestly what they think, and Tolkien says he would never have finished The Lord of the Rings without Jack’s encouragement. The big idea: good friends help each other grow, church is where we belong to God’s family, and God listens when his friends talk together.

memory_verse.text: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

activity.title: Our Own Inklings Story
steps: Sit in a circle like the Inklings round the fire.
Start a story with one sentence, such as “One morning a hedgehog found a key in the garden.”
Go round the circle, each child adding one sentence to the story, until it comes to an end.
Go round once more, each person saying one kind, encouraging thing about someone else’s part of the story.

weeks.summary: When war comes again in 1939, schoolgirls from London come to live at the Kilns, and Jack finds he enjoys them. He writes The Screwtape Letters and gives the money to widows, and his BBC radio talks, explaining plainly what Christians believe, become Mere Christianity; he also learns to use simple words with young airmen. Knowing fame could make him proud, he confesses his sins weekly to a wise priest and gives most of his book money away. The idea of letters from a devil may intrigue or worry children; you only need to say it was a back-to-front way of showing how to follow God. The big idea: you do not need to be clever or famous to share your hope in Jesus, simply and kindly.

memory_verse.text: Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.

activity.title: On the Radio
activity.materials: Nothing (a rolled-up sheet of paper as a pretend microphone, if you like)
steps: Remind the children how Jack talked on the radio in plain, friendly words, like someone at a kitchen table.
In pairs, take turns being the radio speaker and the listener.
As the speaker, say in two or three simple sentences one thing you know or love about Jesus. Anyone who would rather not may say the memory verse instead.
As the listener, say “Thank you for telling me,” then swap.

weeks.summary: Since he was about sixteen Jack had pictured a faun with an umbrella and parcels in a snowy wood; he began a story about four children from London after the evacuees came, and nearly ten years later finished it, and The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe was published in 1950, followed by six more Narnia books. Jack said Aslan was how he imagined the Son of God might be in another world, and he answered children’s letters by hand, telling one worried child that the things he loved about Aslan were the very things Jesus said and did. Meanwhile he kept visiting Mrs Moore until she died in 1951, keeping his promise to the end. The big idea: Jesus loves children and wants everyone to come to him with a simple, trusting heart.

memory_verse.text: And said, most assuredly I tell you, unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

activity.title: A Door into Another World
steps: Draw a tall wardrobe with its door standing a little open.
Through the gap, draw a snowy wood with a lamp-post glowing among the trees.
On the wardrobe door, write or draw one thing Jesus said or did that you love.
Share your pictures, and thank Jesus together for loving children.

weeks.summary: Joy Davidman, a writer in New York who had come to know God one frightening night, writes to Jack, and later moves to England with her sons, David and Douglas. In 1956, so that she can stay in England, Jack marries her in a short ceremony at an office; when she is found to have cancer, he realises he loves her, and in 1957 they are married before God in her hospital room by Peter Bide, who prays for her healing, and to the doctors’ surprise she begins to get better. If children ask about Joy’s first marriage or the two weddings, answer only as simply as the chapter does. The chapter itself says God does not always heal people in the way we ask; hold on to that, as some children will be praying for someone who is ill. The big idea: God always hears our prayers, and we can always bring the people we love to him.

memory_verse.text: I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy.

activity.title: A Praying Hand
steps: Lay one hand flat on a sheet of paper and draw round it with a pencil.
On each finger, write or draw someone to pray for: someone in your family, a friend, someone who is ill, someone who helps you, and yourself.
Hold your paper and pray quietly for each person, one finger at a time.
Take it home and use it to pray during the week.

weeks.summary: Jack and Joy have three happy years together before her cancer returns, and she dies in July 1960 with Jack beside her; he writes his grief honestly in notebooks, later published as A Grief Observed, and gives her sons a home. In 1963 Jack grows ill, unafraid of dying, spends quiet weeks with Warnie, and dies at the Kilns on 22 November 1963; the brothers who made up Boxen are later buried in the same grave. This chapter has two deaths: let it be sad, notice any child who goes quiet, and keep the focus where the chapter does, on God holding on to Jack through happy days and sad ones. The big idea: God holds on to everyone who trusts him, and we can keep the faith all our lives.

memory_verse.text: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.

activity.title: Jack’s Journey
activity.materials: Several sheets of paper laid end to end, and crayons
steps: Lay several sheets of paper in a long line on the floor or a table to make one long path.
Share out the moments of Jack’s life: Boxen in Belfast, the Great Knock, the sidecar ride, the Kilns, the radio talks, the wardrobe, and Jack and Warnie together at the end.
Have each child or pair draw their moment on the path, in order.
Walk along the path together, and at the end write “He kept the faith” and say the memory verse.
